title: Haven't you lived?
hook: "I've done nothing today." What, haven't you lived? (Essays 3.13)

segments.voice: Yesterday, our own bottom: on the highest throne in the world, Montaigne says, we still sit on our own bottom. Your line was my own bottom. Where did your own importance get a laugh? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-two.

Ten-forty at night. The list on the fridge has the same five items it had at breakfast. The inbox is still full. And there's a sentence people say at that hour, out loud or just under their breath: I did nothing today. Montaigne heard that sentence too, and wrote it down in the essay called Of experience. And he answered it with a question so short it almost sounds rude. What, haven't you lived? He doesn't ask what got finished. He asks something stranger. Today, that question.
screen: `THE SAME FIVE ITEMS ON THE LIST.` → `I DID NOTHING TODAY.` → `WHAT, HAVEN'T YOU LIVED?`

segments.voice: First, the complaint. Montaigne calls us great fools, himself included. We say of someone, he spent his life in idleness. We say of ourselves, I've done nothing today. Second, his answer. Haven't you lived? Living, he says, isn't a gap between the real tasks. It's the basic work, and the most excellent of all your occupations. Third, the excuse he hears next, and he hears it clearly. If only I'd been given great affairs, people say, I'd have shown what I could do. And Montaigne turns it around. Have you known how to think about your life and manage it? Then you've done the greatest work there is. Our job, he says, is to compose our character, not to compose books. The great and glorious masterpiece is to live fittingly. Everything else, ruling, piling up money, building, he calls little add-ons and props at most. Notice who's saying this: a man who was, at that moment, composing a book. He isn't against work. He's against the ledger that only counts the work. Fourth, what this looks like in a plain week. You ate a meal. You talked someone through a bad hour. You noticed the light on the wall at four o'clock. You were tired, and you were patient anyway. None of that goes on the list on the fridge. In Montaigne's book, it's the masterpiece.
screen: `I'VE DONE NOTHING TODAY.` · `LIVING IS THE BASIC WORK.` · `COMPOSE YOUR CHARACTER, NOT BOOKS.` · `THE MEAL, THE TALK, THE LIGHT.` · then, large: `THE MASTERPIECE IS TO LIVE FITTINGLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count today as lived. Sit comfortably and let the breath settle. Now go back through today, or yesterday if it's early, not by tasks but by moments. Somewhere you woke. Something you ate or drank. A voice you heard. A moment you were kind, or tried to be. A moment you were simply there. Don't grade any of them. Just set each one down, like coins on a table, and let the pile be what it is. The bell holds the time.
Haven't you lived? Montaigne's answer to the person who says I've done nothing today: living is the basic work, and living fittingly is the masterpiece. Today's word.
Your line: haven't I lived. Tonight, when the list says nothing got done, name three moments from the day that were lived anyway. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Readers of Montaigne often return to this passage from Of experience as a counterweight to measuring a day only by what got finished; some keep it as a short line to say at night.

original.note: Montaigne's French, in the essay Of experience: what, haven't you lived?

trapdoor: what you thought: haven't you lived? is a pep talk.
what it means: Montaigne says living is the basic work, and living fittingly is the masterpiece; the rest are props.
what a scholar hears: it comes in the last essay of the book, from a writer who spent years composing it, and still says character, not books, is the job.

sources.ref: Essays 3.13, Of experience (the complaint 'I have done nothing today'; 'what, have you not lived?'; living as the most excellent occupation; to compose our character, not books; the masterpiece is to live fittingly; ruling, hoarding and building as little appendages and props)

notes: Montaigne is paraphrased throughout; Cotton (1685) and Florio (1603) are public domain but not on the validator's translation list, so nothing is quoted.
'The most excellent of your occupations' paraphrases Montaigne's own superlative ('le plus illustre de vos occupations'); confirm the paraphrase.
Original-language line given as 'Quoi ! avez-vous pas vécu ?'; confirm the exact French of the 1595 text and the pronunciation guide.
The teach mentions he served as a mayor and sat with princes; both come from earlier days of this block (3.10, 3.1), not from 3.13 itself. Cut if the claims editor prefers.
Days 1162–1171 were not on disk when this was written; the review uses the index for day 1171 (our own bottom / my own bottom).
